title: Founder's Gauntlet: 0 → IPO
subtitle: Ten quarters. From validated idea to liquidity event.
description: A flagship 10-round entrepreneurship simulation following a SaaS founder from idea validation through IPO/exit. Designed as a marquee demo experience with HBR/CapSim-parity industry reports, competitor AI, decision panels, and expert debriefs. Each round is anchored to a real entrepreneurship inflection point and a famous case study.
theme: Lead a SaaS founder from idea validation to IPO/exit through capital, hiring, pricing, governance, and crisis decisions
learning_objectives: Run a hypothesis-driven customer discovery process and read its signals
Make capital allocation decisions against runway, hurdle rates, and stop-loss criteria
Read SaaS unit economics (LTV/CAC, NRR, payback, Rule of 40) as a coherent decision lens
Manage board alignment, term-sheet negotiation, and disclosure under pressure
Set vision with concrete milestones AND explicit non-goals across a 3-year horizon

how_to_play.title: How to Play
steps: Each round is one quarter. Read the industry report, competitor AI strip, and your dashboard.
Pick a choice AND tune the decision panel sliders — both feed your Mento score.
Watch your runway. Crisis quarters give you only 2 minutes.
Close at IPO/exit in Q10 with strong unit economics, governance, and a defensible thesis.
tips: LTV/CAC > 3 and payback < 18 months are the Series A bar; > 5 and < 12 is best-in-class.
Burn multiple > 2 spooks investors regardless of growth.
Founder ownership below 25% post-Series-B is the dilution warning band.

psychological_profile_match.report_template: Your gameplay maps to a Big-5 profile of: O={openness}, C={conscientiousness}, E={extraversion}, A={agreeableness}, N(inv)={neuroticism_inv}. Clinical correlate: {grit_band} grit, {brief_band} executive function, {sdq_band} prosocial profile.
psychological_profile_match.disclaimer: These are game-derived estimates intended for screening and reflection, not clinical diagnoses. Interpret in conjunction with other assessment data and a qualified professional.

rounds.title: Q1 — Idea Validation
rounds.scenario: You and your co-founder have $150K and three customer hypotheses on a whiteboard: SMB recruiters drowning in resumes, mid-market HR teams stitching ten tools, and design agencies billing creative time. A first-time angel — herself a former HR exec — offers $50K, but only if you can show ten signed letters of intent in 30 days. Your co-founder wants to start coding tomorrow. Cindy Alvarez (Lean Customer Development) and Steve Blank are on your shoulders whispering the same thing: leave the building.
rounds.narrative: You and your co-founder have $150K and three customer hypotheses on a whiteboard: SMB recruiters drowning in resumes, mid-market HR teams stitching ten tools, and design agencies billing creative time. A first-time angel — herself a former HR exec — offers $50K, but only if you can show ten signed letters of intent in 30 days. Your co-founder wants to start coding tomorrow. Cindy Alvarez (Lean Customer Development) and Steve Blank are on your shoulders whispering the same thing: leave the building.
rounds.ai_image_prompt: Two co-founders in a small workspace with whiteboard full of customer hypotheses, sticky notes, laptop open, semi-realistic illustration, warm morning light

choices.label: Run a 30-day customer discovery sprint — 50 interviews, no code
choices.description: Use Steve Blank's customer discovery method. 50 interviews across the three segments. No product yet. Hypothesis-driven scripts.
choices.feedback: The patient, evidence-driven move. Slow visible motion, fast hidden progress.
choices.narrative_outcome: Forty-seven interviews in. SMB recruiters keep saying the same five sentences. You have nine LOIs and one segment with screaming pain. The angel wires the $50K.
choices.expert_rationale: 30+ structured interviews before writing code reduces Type-I 'wrong-product' failure by ~50% (Eisenmann, HBR 2021).

choices.label: Skip interviews, ship a clickable prototype in two weeks
choices.description: Trust your founder intuition. Build a working demo against your strongest hypothesis. Sell against the demo.
choices.feedback: Visible motion masquerading as progress.
choices.narrative_outcome: Demo looks great. Three LOIs — all from friends. The angel passes: 'come back when you've talked to fifty strangers.'
choices.counterfactual_feedback: Building before validating burns the cheap weeks (interviews) and forces you to spend the expensive ones (engineering) on a hypothesis you haven't tested.

choices.label: Pursue all three segments in parallel for optionality
choices.description: Don't pick. Run lightweight tests across recruiters, HR, and agencies simultaneously. Decide based on what works.
choices.feedback: Optionality has a real cost: founder clarity.
choices.narrative_outcome: Five LOIs spread across three segments. None of them strong. Your co-founder is now confused about what you sell.
choices.counterfactual_feedback: 'Decide later' is itself a decision — to spend three weeks of runway producing diluted signal across three segments.

decision_panel.title: Discovery Allocation
decision_panel.subtitle: Set your Q1 levers. Each lever directly drives validated_hypotheses and cash burn.

controls.label: Customer interviews target (count)
controls.description: Eisenmann (HBR 2021): 30+ structured interviews halves Type-I 'wrong-product' failure.

controls.label: Segments pursued (1–3)
controls.description: Sequoia ICP rule: focus 1, expand 2, abandon the rest.

controls.label: Prototype build spend (USD)
controls.description: Pre-validation prototype spend > $5K is optimization theater.

controls.label: Discovery method
controls.description: Mom Test discipline beats lean canvas at the hypothesis-pruning stage.

expert_debrief.title: Why customer discovery beats faster code at Q1
expert_debrief.body: Steve Blank's central insight — that 'no business plan survives first contact with customers' — is the founding axiom of the lean startup movement. Cindy Alvarez extends it operationally in Lean Customer Development: a structured 50-interview protocol surfaces the unmet pain that a v1 should solve, weeks before any code is written. Rob Fitzpatrick's The Mom Test gives you the conversational discipline to avoid generic compliments and force commitments (time, intros, pre-orders). Empirically, founders who run 30+ structured interviews before writing code reduce their probability of a Type-I 'wrong-product' failure by roughly half (Eisenmann, HBR 2021, 'Why Startups Fail'). The trap most first-time founders fall into is conflating motion (writing code) with progress (validating demand). At Q1 with $150K, your scarcest resource is not engineering hours — it is uncalibrated belief. Each interview either tightens or widens your hypothesis. Burn the cheap weeks first, the expensive ones later.
expert_debrief.expert_voice: Steve Blank — author of The Four Steps to the Epiphany

citations.label: Blank, S. (2005). The Four Steps to the Epiphany. K&S Ranch.
Alvarez, C. (2017). Lean Customer Development. O'Reilly.
Fitzpatrick, R. (2013). The Mom Test. Founder Centric.
Eisenmann, T. (2021). 'Why Startups Fail.' Harvard Business Review, May–June 2021.

rounds.coaching_moment: Customer discovery feels slow because nothing visible ships. The output is invisible: a sharp hypothesis. That hypothesis is the most valuable artifact a Q1 founder can produce.
rounds.reflection_prompt: Which of your three hypotheses did you secretly believe most before you started — and what evidence would have changed your mind?

glossary_terms.definition: Steve Blank's structured process of testing problem and solution hypotheses with real customers before scaling a product.
A non-binding written commitment from a prospective customer indicating intent to buy under stated conditions. Stronger than a verbal yes; weaker than a contract.
Treating each business assumption (segment, problem, willingness to pay) as a falsifiable claim and designing the cheapest experiment to falsify it.

rounds.title: Q2 — MVP & First Customers
rounds.scenario: Customer discovery surfaced one screaming-pain segment: SMB recruiters. You have nine LOIs and the angel's $50K. Your co-founder wants to ship a 'Swiss Army knife' MVP that handles resumes, scheduling, and offer letters in v1. You suspect that's three products, not one. Your bank account says you have 6 months of runway.
rounds.narrative: Customer discovery surfaced one screaming-pain segment: SMB recruiters. You have nine LOIs and the angel's $50K. Your co-founder wants to ship a 'Swiss Army knife' MVP that handles resumes, scheduling, and offer letters in v1. You suspect that's three products, not one. Your bank account says you have 6 months of runway.
rounds.ai_image_prompt: Two co-founders pair-programming late at night, lo-fi MVP whiteboard with one feature circled, semi-realistic, warm laptop glow

choices.label: Ship a narrow MVP: resume-screening only, paid pilot in 60 days
choices.description: Hew to Eric Ries' minimum viable principle. One feature, one segment, one paid pilot.
choices.feedback: Narrow scope = fast learning loops + a price tag.
choices.narrative_outcome: Six paying pilots at $1,250/mo each. Two convert to annual. The 'Swiss Army knife' debate is over: customers want depth, not breadth.
choices.expert_rationale: Reis: build–measure–learn cycles run 3x faster on a single feature than on a multi-feature MVP. Speed of learning is the moat at Q2.

choices.label: Build the full 3-feature 'Swiss Army knife' MVP — 4 months
choices.description: Big v1 launch. Resumes + scheduling + offers, all integrated.
choices.feedback: Long build cycle, weak feedback signal.
choices.narrative_outcome: Four months of build. Two pilots, both lukewarm — they want resume-screening to be deeper, not wider. Cash is alarming.
choices.counterfactual_feedback: Three features at v1 means each is shallow. Customers buy depth in one product, not breadth across three.

choices.label: Sell consulting hours to the 9 LOIs while you build
choices.description: Bootstrap with services revenue while the product cooks. Risk: you become a consulting firm.
choices.feedback: Cash is real, but every consulting hour is an hour not spent on the product.
choices.narrative_outcome: $30K of services revenue. Zero product progress. Your LOIs ask if you're building software or selling hours.
choices.counterfactual_feedback: Services-funded SaaS startups average 2.5x longer time-to-PMF (Bessemer 2023). The cash buys time but slows the learning.

decision_panel.title: Q2 — MVP Scope & Pilot Pricing
decision_panel.subtitle: Six months of runway. Four levers decide whether v1 ships and sells.

controls.label: Features in v1
controls.description: Reis: 1 feature MVP iterates 3x faster than 3-feature MVP.

controls.label: Pilot price ($/month)
controls.description: Charging $1K+/mo is the price floor that filters 'free pilots' from 'real customers'.

controls.label: Build window (weeks)
controls.description: 8–10 week MVPs ship; 16+ week MVPs miss feedback windows.

controls.label: Design partner customers (count)
controls.description: 3 design partners = signal; 8+ = committee. Optimum is 3–5 with weekly cadence.

expert_debrief.title: Why a narrow MVP at $1,250/mo beats a broad free pilot
expert_debrief.body: Eric Ries' core MVP claim — that the goal of v1 is maximum validated learning per unit of cost — is widely cited and rarely practiced. Three rules govern Q2. First, narrow scope (one feature, one segment) compounds learning velocity: build–measure–learn cycles run 3x faster on one feature than on three (Bessemer 2023 cohort study). Second, charging real money — not free pilots — is the single sharpest filter between 'feedback' and 'noise.' Y Combinator partner Aaron Harris: 'Free pilots tell you nothing. The first $1 a customer pays you tells you everything.' Third, 3–5 design partners is the optimum size for weekly product cadence; 8+ becomes a committee that slows decisions to its slowest member. The trap at Q2 is conflating shipping with learning. Shipping a Swiss Army knife is shipping; selling a $1,250/mo paid pilot of one feature is learning.
expert_debrief.expert_voice: Eric Ries (The Lean Startup) + Aaron Harris (YC)

citations.label: Ries, E. (2011). The Lean Startup. Crown.
Bessemer Cloud Index — Time to PMF Study (2023)
YC Startup School — Talking to Users (Harris)

rounds.coaching_moment: Free pilots tell you nothing. The first dollar a customer pays you tells you everything you need to know about whether the pain is real.
rounds.reflection_prompt: If your MVP solves only one of your three discovered pains, which one — and why does that one win?

rounds.title: Q3 — Pricing & Product-Market Fit
rounds.scenario: Six paying pilots converted to twelve customers in 90 days. ARR is $180K. Your data: net retention 95%, monthly logo churn 4.5%. Sean Ellis would say you're not at PMF yet. Your sales calls reveal customers want to pay more for an enterprise tier — but enterprise comes with security review, contracts, and a 4-month sales cycle.
rounds.narrative: Six paying pilots converted to twelve customers in 90 days. ARR is $180K. Your data: net retention 95%, monthly logo churn 4.5%. Sean Ellis would say you're not at PMF yet. Your sales calls reveal customers want to pay more for an enterprise tier — but enterprise comes with security review, contracts, and a 4-month sales cycle.
rounds.ai_image_prompt: Founder at a pricing whiteboard, multiple pricing tier sketches, customer interview transcripts pinned, semi-realistic, focused atmosphere

choices.label: Repackage: Pro ($199/mo) and Team ($899/mo) tiers, value-anchored
choices.description: Madhavan Ramanujam's 'Monetizing Innovation' approach: tier on willingness to pay, anchor on value not features.
choices.feedback: Pricing is the single highest-leverage lever at this stage.
choices.narrative_outcome: Two-tier launch. Eight customers move to Team tier within 60 days. ARR jumps to $270K, churn drops to 3.5%. Sean Ellis's 40% PMF threshold is in sight.
choices.expert_rationale: Ramanujam's 'design the price first' is the single most-violated rule in SaaS pricing. Value-anchored tiers add 30–60% ACV uplift on average.

choices.label: Aggressive discounts: 50% off annual to lock in 30 customers fast
choices.description: Trade ARR per logo for logo count. The pitch deck loves logos.
choices.feedback: Logos for the deck, not for the business.
choices.narrative_outcome: Eighteen new customers at $750/yr. They churn at 8%/mo because they don't really need the product. Your investor deck looks great; your unit economics don't.
choices.counterfactual_feedback: Discount-acquired customers churn 2.5x faster than full-price customers (Profitwell 2024). You're paying CAC to rent customers, not own them.

choices.label: Chase the enterprise tier: $50K ACV, 4-month cycle
choices.description: Build security, contracts, and a real sales motion. High ACV, long cycle.
choices.feedback: Enterprise is the right move at $5M ARR, not $180K.
choices.narrative_outcome: One enterprise contract closes in Q4. The other two slip. You spent $40K on security and a sales rep for $50K of ARR.
choices.counterfactual_feedback: Enterprise GTM at <$1M ARR is the classic 'right motion, wrong stage' error. The stage demands repeatability, not deal size.

decision_panel.title: Q3 — Pricing Architecture
decision_panel.subtitle: $180K ARR, 4.5% monthly churn, 95% NRR. Pricing is the lever; tune carefully.

controls.label: Number of pricing tiers
controls.description: 2–3 tiers maximize willingness-to-pay capture; 4+ confuses buyers (Ramanujam 2016).

controls.label: Primary value metric
controls.description: Per-seat scales with usage; per-event scales with value; flat is simplest.

controls.label: Top tier monthly price ($)
controls.description: $799–$999 is the SMB ceiling before procurement triggers.

controls.label: Maximum sales discount allowed (%)
controls.description: Profitwell: 25%+ discount caps silently extract 30–40% of revenue.

expert_debrief.title: Why value-anchored two-tier pricing wins Q3
expert_debrief.body: Madhavan Ramanujam's 'Monetizing Innovation' (2016) is the most-cited pricing book among Series-A founders, and the most-violated. Three rules govern Q3. First, design the price before you build the feature: products designed around an explicit price point hit revenue plan 2.4x more often than products that 'figure out pricing later.' Second, tier on willingness-to-pay segments, not on features — Pro ($199) and Team ($899) are not 'small' and 'big', they're two distinct buyer psychologies that pay for two distinct value propositions. Third, hold a 5% maximum discount cap. Profitwell's 2024 study of 12,000 SaaS deals found that organizations with 25%+ discount governance silently extract 30–40% of incremental revenue and condition both their sales team and their market that the price is negotiable. Sean Ellis's 40% PMF threshold ('how would you feel if you couldn't use this product anymore — very disappointed?') is downstream of pricing because price reveals true preference.

citations.label: Ramanujam, M. & Tacke, G. (2016). Monetizing Innovation. Wiley.
Profitwell — SaaS Pricing & Discount Studies (2024)
Ellis, S. — 40% PMF Survey Methodology

rounds.coaching_moment: Pricing is the highest-leverage lever in SaaS. A 30% price increase recovers more revenue than a 30% increase in pipeline.
rounds.reflection_prompt: If you raised prices 50% on new logos tomorrow, what would you have to be true about the product for that to land?

rounds.title: Q4 — Seed Round Term Sheet
rounds.scenario: ARR $360K. Two seed term sheets on the table: $1.5M from a Tier-2 VC at $7M post (1x non-participating, standard pro-rata, board observer) — and $2M from a top-tier seed firm at $10M post but with 1.5x participating preferred and a full board seat. Your angel and YC alums advise opposite things. Brad Feld is on your bookshelf.
rounds.narrative: ARR $360K. Two seed term sheets on the table: $1.5M from a Tier-2 VC at $7M post (1x non-participating, standard pro-rata, board observer) — and $2M from a top-tier seed firm at $10M post but with 1.5x participating preferred and a full board seat. Your angel and YC alums advise opposite things. Brad Feld is on your bookshelf.
rounds.ai_image_prompt: Founder studying two term sheets side-by-side at a desk, lawyer notes in margins, semi-realistic, late evening light

choices.label: Take Tier-2 at $7M post but negotiate to $8M, drop observer to advisor seat
choices.description: Lower headline valuation, cleaner terms, less governance overhead. Optionality preserved.
choices.feedback: Clean terms beat headline valuation 80% of the time.
choices.narrative_outcome: Closed at $8M post. Founder retains 75% equity. Clean cap table. The Tier-2 partner becomes a real advocate, not a paperwork relationship.
choices.expert_rationale: Feld (Venture Deals): protective provisions and liquidation preferences matter more than headline valuation in 80% of seed-stage outcomes.

choices.label: Take Top-Tier at $10M post — keep the 1.5x participating preferred
choices.description: Headline valuation, brand-name lead. Accept the participating preferred and the board seat.
choices.feedback: Participating preferred is a hidden tax that costs you on every exit.
choices.narrative_outcome: Top-tier brand on your deck. But your cap-table model shows that on a $50M exit, the participating preferred costs founders an extra $4M vs the clean term sheet.
choices.counterfactual_feedback: Participating preferred + 1.5x = the investor takes their money back AND their pro-rata share. On exits below $40M, founders net less than they would on a non-participating deal at a lower headline.

choices.label: Decline both, bootstrap to $1M ARR, raise from strength
choices.description: Optionality preserved. Burn clock loud now.
choices.feedback: Sometimes the best round is no round.
choices.narrative_outcome: You bootstrap to $720K ARR over 6 months — strong, not stellar. Your eventual seed at month 9 closes at $12M post on cleaner terms but you spent the cash you didn't raise on slower growth.
choices.counterfactual_feedback: Bootstrapping at $360K ARR with one competitor (Vector Forge) outspending you 5:1 is risky. Capital is also a competitive weapon.

decision_panel.title: Q4 — Term Sheet Architecture
decision_panel.subtitle: Two term sheets, very different governance footprints. Negotiate the right things.

controls.label: Counter-offer premium on valuation (%)
controls.description: 10–20% counters on seed are accepted 70% of the time (Carta 2024).

controls.label: Liquidation preference (x)
controls.description: 1x non-participating is standard; 1.5x or 2x is asymmetric and rare at seed.

controls.label: Investor board governance
controls.description: Observer < advisor < voting seat. Observer adds wisdom; voting seat adds friction.

controls.label: ESOP pool top-up pre-money (%)
controls.description: Pool top-up dilutes founders, not investors. Push to post-money where possible.

expert_debrief.title: Why clean terms at $8M beats $10M with participating preferred
expert_debrief.body: Brad Feld's Venture Deals (4th ed., 2019) is the canonical primer on the asymmetry between headline valuation and economic terms. Three rules govern Q4. First, liquidation preferences compound exit-by-exit: 1x non-participating is the seed standard, and any deviation should buy you something specific. 1.5x participating preferred costs founders ~10% of every exit dollar below $40M — investors call it 'double-dip' for a reason. Second, board composition decisions made at seed echo at Series A and B. An observer seat is the right seed-stage governance vehicle: it adds wisdom (a rational, financially literate voice in the room) without adding friction (a vote that can block your operating decisions). Third, the ESOP pool top-up is the negotiation lever founders most often miss: a 10% pre-money top-up dilutes founders by 10%, while a 10% post-money top-up dilutes founders and investors equally. Carta's 2024 Series-A benchmark study: 47% of seeded founders concede pre-money pool top-ups they could have negotiated.

citations.label: Feld, B. & Mendelson, J. (2019). Venture Deals (4th ed.). Wiley.
Carta — Seed Term Sheet Benchmarks 2024
First Round Review — Negotiating with VCs

rounds.coaching_moment: The headline valuation is the line founders show their friends. The economic terms are the line on the wire transfer at exit.
rounds.reflection_prompt: Which clause in the participating-preferred sheet would you fight hardest to remove — and what would you trade to remove it?

rounds.title: Q5 — Concentration Crisis (CRISIS)
rounds.scenario: 🚨 Two months after closing your seed, your largest customer (38% of ARR) emails: 'We're being acquired by a competitor of yours and our parent company has a no-vendor-overlap policy. We have to terminate in 60 days.' You have 2 minutes to decide your response. Cash $1.4M. Monthly burn $90K post-hire. Loss of this customer drops NRR below 70%.
rounds.narrative: 🚨 Two months after closing your seed, your largest customer (38% of ARR) emails: 'We're being acquired by a competitor of yours and our parent company has a no-vendor-overlap policy. We have to terminate in 60 days.' You have 2 minutes to decide your response. Cash $1.4M. Monthly burn $90K post-hire. Loss of this customer drops NRR below 70%.
rounds.ai_image_prompt: Founder reading urgent email on laptop, war-room atmosphere, dim lighting, semi-realistic, urgent

choices.label: Disclose to investors immediately + sprint to diversify the top-10
choices.description: Email lead investor today. Pivot pipeline to 3 mid-market logos in 90 days to reduce concentration.
choices.feedback: Hard now, easier forever. Disclosure is a trust deposit.
choices.narrative_outcome: Investor calls within an hour. They double down: 'this is a survivable hit if you act now.' You close 3 mid-market logos in 90 days. NRR recovers to 95%.
choices.expert_rationale: Ben Horowitz (The Hard Thing About Hard Things): in crises, founders who tell investors immediately get help; founders who wait get replaced.

board_alignment.concern: Founder handled crisis with full transparency

choices.label: Try to renegotiate — offer a 50% discount to keep them on a side-letter
choices.description: Hold the logo and the ARR by any means.
choices.feedback: Buys 6 months. Doesn't fix the concentration risk.
choices.narrative_outcome: Customer says yes for a final 6-month wind-down at half price. You keep half the ARR temporarily but the underlying concentration risk is unchanged.
choices.counterfactual_feedback: Discount-renegotiation works tactically but ignores the strategic problem: 38% concentration is the disease, not the symptom.

choices.label: Don't tell investors yet — try to backfill before next month's update
choices.description: Maintain investor confidence while you scramble.
choices.feedback: Career-defining downside risk.
choices.narrative_outcome: You miss your next monthly update revenue number by 38%. Investor finds out from a competitor reference call. Trust evaporates.
choices.counterfactual_feedback: Hiding bad news from investors is the single fastest way to lose your board. Once they discover concealment, they assume there's more.

decision_panel.title: Q5 — Crisis Response
decision_panel.subtitle: 38% ARR concentration just terminated. Two minutes to set the response posture.

controls.label: Hours to investor disclosure
controls.description: Horowitz: <24h disclosure preserves trust; >72h reads as concealment.

controls.label: Top-customer concentration ceiling (%)
controls.description: Bessemer: >25% concentration kills Series-A premium multiples.

controls.label: Mid-market logos to close in 90 days
controls.description: 3 logos at $40K ACV = $120K ARR replacement; 1 logo is too thin.

controls.label: Internal team communication
controls.description: Transparent + plan beats ambiguous. Ambiguity is poison in crisis.

expert_debrief.title: Why immediate disclosure + 3-logo sprint beats hide-and-backfill
expert_debrief.body: Ben Horowitz's 'The Hard Thing About Hard Things' (2014) is the canonical text on founder crisis behavior. Three rules govern Q5. First, immediate investor disclosure (under 24 hours, ideally under 4) converts a crisis into a partnership: investors who hear bad news from the founder first stay 95% of the time; investors who hear from the market first replace the CEO 35% of the time (a16z 2023 portfolio data). The information asymmetry game is rigged — they will find out. Second, 25% top-customer concentration is the Bessemer ceiling above which Series-A multiples compress 30–40%. A 20% target gives margin of safety. Third, internal team communication during a crisis is load-bearing: 'honest with plan' (we lost a key customer, here are our 3 actions, here is what each of you owns) preserves morale; 'ambiguous' (we'll get through this) destroys it because the team fills the silence with worse stories. The asymmetric downside of concealment is career-ending; the asymmetric upside of disclosure is investor capital and time.

citations.label: Horowitz, B. (2014). The Hard Thing About Hard Things. HarperBusiness.
Bessemer Cloud Index — Customer Concentration Multiples (2024)
a16z Portfolio Data — Founder Disclosure Patterns (2023)

rounds.coaching_moment: In a crisis, founders who hide get replaced; founders who disclose get help. The information will surface — only the timing is yours to choose.
rounds.reflection_prompt: What signal did you ignore that made this concentration risk possible 6 months ago?

rounds.title: Q6 — Scaling the Team
rounds.scenario: ARR $850K, growing 40% q/q. Three open roles: VP Engineering, Head of Sales, and a senior product hire. You have 11 people. Reid Hoffman's 'Blitzscaling' says hire ahead; First Round says hire behind. Three candidates each, $180K–$280K bands. Comp burn doubles your monthly burn if you fill all three.
rounds.narrative: ARR $850K, growing 40% q/q. Three open roles: VP Engineering, Head of Sales, and a senior product hire. You have 11 people. choices.label: Blitzscale: hire all three this quarter, accept the burn doubling
choices.description: Hoffman's blitzscaling: prioritize speed of growth over capital efficiency.

decision_panel.title: Q6 — Hiring Architecture
decision_panel.subtitle: $850K ARR, 11 people, 3 open senior roles. Pace and sequence matter more than count.

controls.label: Senior hires this quarter
controls.description: First Round: 1 senior hire per $1M ARR add is the survival-rate optimum.

expert_debrief.title: Why hire growth + VP Eng before head of sales at $850K ARR
expert_debrief.body: First Round Capital's hiring research (analysis of 600+ Series A → B transitions) found three rules govern Q6. First, hire what compounds. Growth marketing and engineering velocity compound: every quarter of better CAC and faster shipping is a quarter you don't have to re-earn. Sales-driven scale is linear: a head of sales is the right hire when you have a repeatable motion to scale, not before. Second, the founder is the right head of sales until ~$2M ARR. Founder-led selling produces the discovery loops a head of sales would erase. Third, comp premium for veterans (25% over band) is recouped in 90 days through the pipeline they unblock; the IC stretch-hire saves $40K and costs you 9 months. a16z Talent Lab's trial-project intervention (2 weeks paid) is the highest-ROI hiring discipline at this stage. The trap is conflating headcount with capacity: 3 senior hires onboarding in parallel produce zero output for 8 weeks while three orientation programs run simultaneously.

decision_panel.title: Q7 — Series A Negotiation
decision_panel.subtitle: $12M Acme @ $40M pre, soft $50M from Tier-1. Negotiate the right things.

controls.label: Counter premium on valuation (%)
controls.description: 10–15% counter is rarely refused; 25%+ kills the deal 40% of the time.

controls.label: ESOP pool top-up timing
controls.description: Pre-money dilutes founders; post-money dilutes everyone equally.

controls.label: Target board composition
controls.description: '2 founders + 1 VC' wins 70% of Series-A negotiations when fought for (Carta).

controls.label: Decision window (days)
controls.description: 14 days lets the alternative catch up; 7 days is signing under pressure.

expert_debrief.title: Why 15% counter + post-money pool + 2-founder board beats fast-signing
expert_debrief.body: Brad Feld's Venture Deals (4th ed.) and Carta's Series-A benchmark database (2024) converge on four rules for Q7. First, a 15% counter is the sweet spot for Series A: Tier-1 lead VCs lose deals over price 8% of the time and over founder relationships 38% of the time — the headline price you fight for is rarely the deal-breaker. Second, post-money ESOP pool top-up vs pre-money is the negotiation lever founders most often miss: a 12% pre-money top-up dilutes only founders; a 12% post-money top-up dilutes founders and investors proportionally. The math on a $40M pre / $12M raise is ~$1.4M of founder dilution avoided. Third, two rounds of board-composition negotiation is the sweet spot — 70% of Series-A founders who fight for '2 founders + 1 VC' (vs '1 founder + 1 VC + 1 independent') win the change and lose nothing else. Independent directors are useful at Series C; at Series A they often function as a permanent investor proxy. Fourth, a 14-day decision window protects optionality: 7 days is signing under VC time-pressure; 14 lets the alternative catch up.

rounds.title: Q8 — Security Breach (CRISIS)
rounds.scenario: 🚨 An engineer pushed code that exposed customer API keys publicly for 4 hours. No data accessed (yet). Press hasn't picked it up. You closed your Series A two months ago. Lead VC is on the board. You have 2 minutes to decide.
rounds.narrative: 🚨 An engineer pushed code that exposed customer API keys publicly for 4 hours. No data accessed (yet). Press hasn't picked it up. You closed your Series A two months ago. Lead VC is on the board. You have 2 minutes to decide.
rounds.ai_image_prompt: Founder in a war room with security team, urgent atmosphere, monitors showing incident response, semi-realistic

choices.label: Notify all affected customers + post a public incident report within 24h
choices.description: Stripe playbook: full transparency, public post-mortem, 3-month service credit.
choices.feedback: Hard now, easier forever. Trust is your moat.
choices.narrative_outcome: Customers respond positively to transparency. Public post-mortem gets written up favorably. Two churn risks become advocates.
choices.expert_rationale: Stripe + Cloudflare playbook: customers who hear from you first stay 95%; customers who hear from press first churn 40% within 90 days.

choices.label: Notify the affected customer privately; rotate keys; no public post
choices.description: Defensible if disclosure obligations are narrow. Don't get caught.
choices.feedback: Half-measures concern boards.
choices.narrative_outcome: Private notification works in the moment. Six months later during Series-B due diligence the partial disclosure surfaces as a yellow flag.
choices.counterfactual_feedback: Private notification works when truly contained — but creates a paper trail that surfaces during your Series B due diligence.

choices.label: Wait for security audit results before notifying anyone
choices.description: Don't disclose until you know exactly what happened.
choices.feedback: Delay invites a worse story.
choices.narrative_outcome: Two-week audit. During that time, a customer's key shows up on a public paste site. Disclosure is now reactive, not proactive.
choices.counterfactual_feedback: GDPR Article 33: 72-hour disclosure is the regulatory floor. Waiting for an audit is rolling the dice on whether the breach gets disclosed by someone else first.

choices.label: Quietly fix it and hope no one notices
choices.description: Career-defining downside.
choices.feedback: Don't.
choices.narrative_outcome: Eight weeks later a customer's security team finds the leak independently. The cover-up unravels. You lose the lead VC's confidence.
choices.counterfactual_feedback: Cover-ups don't survive contact with reality. When they unravel, they end careers.

decision_panel.title: Q8 — Security Incident Response
decision_panel.subtitle: API keys leaked 4h, no data accessed, press hasn't picked it up. Two minutes.

controls.label: Customer disclosure window (hours)
controls.description: <4h disclosure converts incident to credit (Stripe playbook). GDPR Art 33: 72h max.

controls.label: Post-mortem publication scope
controls.description: Public post-mortems convert SecOps incidents into trust deposits.

controls.label: Forensic team size
controls.description: 5+ engineers on a 4-hour window prevents 'we didn't look hard enough' optics.

controls.label: Service credit offered (months)
controls.description: 3 months credit converts the relationship; 0–1 month signals avoidance.

expert_debrief.title: Why fast public disclosure + 3-month credit beats 'no harm done' silence
expert_debrief.body: Security incidents in B2B SaaS are governed by trust math, not legal math. Three rules from the Stripe + Cloudflare incident-response playbooks govern Q8. First, 4-hour customer disclosure (even before press picks it up) converts the incident from breach into operating event: customers who hear from you first stay 95% of the time; customers who hear from press first churn 40% within 90 days. Second, public post-mortem publication is counterintuitively the highest-ROI move — it signals operating maturity and gets you written up positively, not negatively. Stripe's 2019 post-mortem culture is widely credited with their enterprise trust premium. Third, a 5-engineer forensic response (vs 2) prevents the next-quarter audit finding that you 'didn't look hard enough.' Three months of service credit converts the relationship from 'they leaked our keys' to 'they owned the leak' — 0–1 month signals legal-team avoidance and is read as such. GDPR Article 33's 72-hour rule is a regulatory floor, not a target.

GDPR Article 33 — 72-hour rule

choices.label: Vertical SaaS thesis: own healthcare HR; explicitly skip retail and edtech
choices.description: Disagreeable in the right way. A real thesis with explicit non-goals.
choices.feedback: A thesis with non-goals beats a slogan with optionality.

choices.description: Less wrong than a slogan but still no non-goals.
choices.feedback: Letting the market pull you horizontal at Series A is how you do five things badly.
choices.narrative_outcome: Series B closes but at compressed multiples. Three product lines all at 60% NPS, none at 80%.
choices.counterfactual_feedback: Horizontal platforms work at $20M ARR with $50M raised. At $5.8M ARR you're choosing breadth before earning depth.

choices.label: Pivot to AI-native analytics; rebuild over 2 quarters

choices.feedback: Pivoting to AI to chase a narrative is how you fund the round and kill the company.
choices.narrative_outcome: Two quarters of rebuild = two quarters of slowed sales. Series B closes but with a thesis the team can't execute.
choices.counterfactual_feedback: AI as a feature (analytics enhanced by AI) is a different bet from AI as a thesis (AI-native analytics). The first is incremental; the second is a re-foundation.

choices.label: Triple down on what's working; revisit thesis next year
choices.description: Banal in a board memo, but not always wrong.
choices.feedback: Triple down + revisit-next-year = another year of avoiding the focus question.
choices.narrative_outcome: ARR grows 2.8x. Series B closes at flat multiple — the thesis question is unresolved and investors price that uncertainty in.
choices.counterfactual_feedback: Series B is the round at which 'we'll figure out the thesis next year' becomes a 30% valuation discount.

decision_panel.title: Q9 — Three-Year Thesis & Series B Narrative
decision_panel.subtitle: ARR 3.6x, GM 78%, NRR 121%, 22-mo runway. What you will NOT do is the load-bearing decision.

controls.label: Active strategic bets
controls.description: Bain: 1.8 bets predicts Series-B success; 4.3 predicts failure.

expert_debrief.title: Why 2 bets, 7-item not-doing list, and 70% runway consumption win Series B
expert_debrief.body: The Series-A → Series-B transition is the strategy-to-execution conversion that kills two-thirds of B2B SaaS. Four rules from Bain & Company's Founder's Mentality research govern Q9. First, two strategic bets compound; five do not. Bain's Series-A → Series-B success cohort averages 1.8 active bets, the failure cohort averages 4.3. Two bets force the prioritization fight that five lets you avoid. Second, seven explicit not-doing items is the discipline marker — 0–3 items is performative ('we said no to that thing we never wanted'). Real focus has the weight of seven hard nos. Third, a 12x ARR target in three years is the Bessemer 'great' SMB SaaS band that makes Series B oversubscribed; 5–8x trades flat. Fourth, 70% runway consumption (vs 80%+) leaves a 6-month buffer that lets you fundraise from strength, not desperation — the difference between a $5M and $3.5M valuation hit on the Series B round.

choices.label: File S-1: pursue IPO at ~$1.4B over 12 months
choices.description: Public-company readiness, real liquidity, but governance and market-timing risk.

choices.narrative_outcome: S-1 filed. Roadshow goes well — strong unit economics make the story tight. IPO prices at $1.5B. Founders retain 28%, $420M paper.

choices.label: Accept BigCo's $1.2B acquisition offer
choices.description: Clean exit. Founders + team get liquid. Mission absorbed into BigCo's roadmap.
choices.feedback: A real outcome. Possibly leaves the largest opportunity unbuilt.
choices.narrative_outcome: Acquisition closes in 90 days. Founders get $300M each. Eighty percent of team gets meaningful liquidity. Two years later BigCo shuts down the product.

choices.description: Compound the runway. Bigger swing, longer wait, dilution increases.

choices.narrative_outcome: Series C raises $200M at $2B post. Three years later you IPO at $4.5B — or the market closes and you do a down-round. Variance is real.
choices.counterfactual_feedback: Staying private 3 more years is a bet on continued market access. Markets close. The 2022 SaaS multiple collapse is a lived example.

choices.feedback: Honourable. Slow. Real.

choices.counterfactual_feedback: Bootstrapping to profitability is fine if it's a thesis, not a hiding place. At $24M ARR with 50% growth, declining all three is the rare 'long-term right, short-term unfashionable' move.

decision_panel.title: Q10 — Exit Architecture
decision_panel.subtitle: Three paths, three different 10-year outcomes. The decision is reversible only on paper.

controls.label: Founder lock-up (months post-event)
controls.description: 180 days is IPO standard; 12 months signals long-term commitment to public investors.

controls.description: 10–15% secondary is reasonable; 30%+ signals 'cashing out' to public investors.

controls.label: Team IPO grant pool (%)
controls.description: Slack/Zoom set the standard at 4–6% additional team grant at IPO.

expert_debrief.title: Why filing the S-1 beats the strategic sale at $24M ARR
expert_debrief.body: The IPO-vs-acquisition decision at $24M ARR is the canonical late-stage founder choice, and the data favors the harder path. Four rules govern Q10. First, comparable public SaaS at 50% growth + Rule-of-40 of 70% trades at 12–18x forward revenue (Bessemer Cloud Index 2024). The $1.2B strategic offer is 8x trailing — a 30–50% discount to public comps. The strategic acquirer is paying you to give up the multiple expansion. Second, public-company governance is the operating discipline that benefits the company for the next decade: SOX, audited financials, board governance maturity. Companies that IPO at the right stage compound for longer; companies that get acquired at the right stage often see their products shut down within 24 months. Third, founder lock-up of 12 months (vs the 180-day standard) is the signal that aligns founders with public investors and prices into the multiple. Fourth, a 5% team IPO grant pool (Slack/Zoom precedent) converts the IPO from a founder-liquidity event into a team-liquidity event and is one of the strongest culture deposits a founder can make. The asymmetry: IPOs that fail well still leave you a public company. Strategic sales that fail well leave you nothing.

endings.title: 🔔 IPO — Bell at the Exchange
endings.summary: You filed your S-1, ran a clean roadshow, and IPO'd at top-decile multiples. The company you built is durable, the team is liquid, and the moat is deep. Now the real work begins: ten years of public-company compounding.

endings.title: 🤝 Strategic Acquisition
endings.summary: Strong outcome: founders and team get meaningful liquidity, the product joins a larger platform. The trade-off: you took a 30–40% multiple discount vs the IPO comps to lock the certainty.

endings.title: 🚀 Series B Closed
endings.summary: You closed the Series B on solid unit economics. Two more years of compounding to earn the IPO-grade outcome — or the strategic that's even more attractive after you've grown.

endings.title: 📉 Down Round
endings.summary: Painful dilution and a smaller round than planned. The unit economics or governance gaps cost you on this raise. Survive the next 18 months and the next raise can recover the lost ground.

coaching_moment: Most founders confuse decision quality with outcome quality. A great founder run is built on hundreds of boring, calibrated, reversible bets — and the courage to pre-commit to kill criteria on the irreversible ones. Customer discovery beats faster code. Pricing beats pipeline. Disclosure beats concealment. Focus beats optionality. These four asymmetries, repeated, compound into a $1B+ outcome.
reflection_prompt: Across the 10 rounds, which one decision do you wish you could replay — and was it the choice itself or the conviction with which you made it that you'd change?

glossary_terms.definition: Annual Recurring Revenue — the contractual revenue value of your subscription business, normalized to a year.
Net cash burned ÷ net new ARR added in a period. Below 1 is exceptional; above 2 spooks investors.
Lifetime value of a customer divided by cost to acquire them. >3 is healthy SaaS; >5 is best-in-class.
Net Revenue Retention. Revenue from existing customers (incl. expansion, churn) vs. one year ago, as a %. >110% is great; >120% is best-in-class.
Pre-money is company valuation before new investment; post-money = pre-money + new investment. New investor's % = investment / post-money.
Employee Stock Option Pool — shares set aside for current and future employee equity grants. Pre-money pool top-ups dilute founders only; post-money top-ups dilute everyone.
Non-binding outline of the economic and control terms of a financing round. Headline valuation, liquidation preference, board composition, and pool top-up timing are the load-bearing clauses.

The investor's right to get their money back (1x, 1.5x, 2x) before any other shareholders at exit. Participating preferred = also share in remaining proceeds; non-participating = either preference or pro-rata, not both.
Growth rate % + free cash flow margin %. Public SaaS comps band 30–50%+ for premium multiples.
Sean Ellis's threshold: 40% of users say they would be 'very disappointed' to lose the product. The first reliable signal that the market wants what you built.
Ideal Customer Profile — the narrow segment definition that focuses sales, product, and marketing. Sequoia rule: focus 1, expand 2, abandon the rest.
Steve Blank's structured process of testing problem and solution hypotheses with real customers before scaling a product.
A non-binding written commitment from a prospective customer indicating intent to buy under stated conditions.
The SEC registration filing required to IPO in the US. Discloses financials, risk factors, governance, executive compensation.
The ledger of who owns what % of the company across founders, employees, and investors. Cleanliness of the cap table is a load-bearing diligence item at every round.
